hints: First determine the minimum total price.
Keep only edges that can appear on a minimum-price route.
Positive flight prices make the retained graph acyclic in increasing distance order.
analogy: Erase every flight that cannot lie on a cheapest itinerary, then find checkpoints shared by all remaining itineraries.
example: If cheapest routes are 1-2-3-4 and 1-3-4, cities 1, 3 and 4 are unavoidable.
algorithm: Run Dijkstra from 1 and on reversed edges from n. Keep edge u->v of price w only when dist1[u]+w+distN[v]=dist1[n]. Process retained vertices in increasing dist1 order. The immediate dominator of a vertex is the lowest common ancestor, in the dominator tree built so far, of all its retained predecessors. Maintain binary lifting for these LCA queries. The ancestors of n in this tree are the answer; sort them by city number.
correctness: The distance equality characterizes exactly edges on shortest routes. Prices are positive, so retained edges strictly increase dist1 and form a DAG. In a DAG, a vertex is on every path to v exactly when it dominates all predecessors of v; their deepest common dominator is their LCA in the already-built dominator tree. Thus the ancestors of n are precisely the required cities.
complexity: For n cities and m flights, Dijkstra and dominator LCA processing take O((n+m) log n) time and O((n+m) log n) space.
